Assessment Guide

Research Journal

What we're looking for, how we mark it, and what strong entries look like.

Weighting 30%
Entries 4 × ~300 words
Total ~1,200 words or equivalent
Drafts Throughout semester
Final submission Assessment period
Overview

The task

Across the semester, you'll produce a research journal of four entries. Each entry responds to material from the subject modules — specifically, to the provocations embedded in the FeedbackFruits interactive videos. These provocations are your starting points: they'll ask you to engage with a particular moment, idea, or argument from the videos and readings. Your job is to take that starting point and develop it — to think with the material, bring in at least two external sources of your own, and arrive at a position that is genuinely yours.

You choose which four modules to respond to (out of eight). Each entry is approximately 300 words, or its equivalent if you're working in a non-written format.

Entries 1–3 are standalone responses to different module groups — they don't need to connect to one another. Entry 4 is where you draw threads together, making connections across the semester and showing how your thinking has developed.

The journal builds the toolkit. The IOA is where you use it. Your journal entries are about the ideas, practices, and language of theatre — not about the two MTC productions you attend. The productions are the focus of the oral assessment. But the sharper your journal work, the more confidently you'll walk into that conversation.

Assessment criteria

How we mark the journal

The journal is marked out of 100 (weighted to 30% of your final grade). There are five criteria, each assessing something distinct.

01
Peer Engagement
Giving and receiving feedback that engages with ideas
15%
▾

When reviewing a peer's draft, you engage with the substance of their ideas: you might question an assumption, suggest a source that complicates their argument, point to a connection they haven't made, or identify where their thinking could go further. In return, your final submission shows evidence that you've read and responded to the feedback you received — not by accepting every suggestion, but by visibly grappling with it.

02
Engagement with Module Content
Thinking with the provocations, not just about them
20%
▾

Each entry grows out of specific provocations and material from the module videos. We can see that you've done the modules — not by summarising what was said, but by thinking with it: responding to a particular argument a practitioner made, picking up on a tension between two ideas in a video, or following a question that a provocation raised. The provocations are your starting points, and the specificity of your engagement is what tells us you've actually spent time with the material.

03
Research and Discovery
Going beyond the modules with at least two external sources
25%
▾

You go beyond the module materials. Each entry brings in at least two external sources — critics, scholars, practitioners, reviewers — and introduces key theatrical terms and concepts with accuracy. Your sources should be in dialogue with your own thinking: a critic's argument that supports or challenges your position, a practitioner's account of their process that sheds light on something you encountered in a video, a scholarly concept that gives you language for what you're observing. The point is not to reference for the sake of referencing, but to show that your research is shaping how you think about the material.

04
Developing a Position
Arriving at an argument that is recognisably yours
25%
▾

Each entry moves beyond describing or reporting what you've encountered and works toward a position that is recognisably yours. You interrogate the ideas rather than summarising them — questioning, pushing back, making connections, following a thread to see where it leads. Entries 1–3 each arrive at their own standalone argument or stance. Entry 4 draws connections across the semester, showing how your thinking has developed and where you've landed.

05
Presentation and Referencing
Clear structure, cohesive format, accurate referencing
15%
▾

Your journal is clearly structured and your chosen format — whether written, illustrated, video, or a combination — is executed with care and coherence. If you write, your prose is clear and your ideas are well organised. If you work visually, your annotations and captions make your thinking legible — a reader should be able to follow your argument through the image as clearly as through a paragraph. If you work in video, your spoken response should be structured and purposeful, not a stream of consciousness. For all formats, sources are referenced using Chicago 17 Author–Date style — in written work this means in-text citations and a bibliography; in video, a spoken or on-screen citation with a written reference list appended; in visual work, a reference list attached to the submission. You meet the 1,200-word limit (or equivalent) within a 10% margin.

Format and creativity

How you can present your thinking

This is a subject about theatre, and we welcome creativity in how you present your thinking. You may write, illustrate, record a video journal, or combine formats. The intellectual expectations are the same regardless of medium.

Written
Prose, annotation, critical reflection — whatever written form suits your thinking.
Illustrated
Sketches, annotated screenshots, concept maps, diagrammatic responses.
Video journal
Talk through your ideas on camera, with images or objects.
Mixed
Combine formats across entries, or within a single entry.

Written entries: Around 300 words per entry. Reference your sources using Chicago 17 Author–Date with a bibliography at the end of the journal.

Illustrated entries: Illustration means thinking visually — not decoration. You might annotate a moment from a video, map the relationship between two ideas, or diagram a process a practitioner described. Include a brief written caption or annotation that makes your thinking legible, and append a reference list for any sources you draw on.

Video entries: Aim for approximately 2–3 minutes per entry. Your spoken response should be structured and purposeful, not a stream of consciousness — think of it as a spoken entry with the same rigour you'd bring to a written one. Include a spoken or on-screen bibliography, or append a written reference list.

Mixed formats: One entry might be written; another might be a video; a third might be an annotated visual with a paragraph of commentary. The key question is always: does the format serve the ideas?

Whatever format you choose, the same expectation applies: close engagement with the module content, evidence of independent research, and your own thinking visible throughout.

Suggested framework

How to structure an entry

There is no single correct structure, but here is a framework that works well for a 300-word entry. Adapt it to suit your format and thinking.

01
Start from the provocation
~50 words
Name the provocation or moment from the module that sparked your entry. What struck you? What question did it raise? Don't summarise the whole video — land on the specific thing you want to think about.
02
Develop your response
~100 words
Respond directly to what caught your attention. What do you think about it? Why does it matter? Bring in your first external source — a critic, scholar, practitioner, or reviewer — to support, challenge, or contextualise your thinking. Introduce any theatrical terms or concepts you're drawing on.
03
Deepen and complicate
~100 words
Push further. Bring in your second external source to develop your argument. This is where you show a deeper understanding of the relevant ideas, debates, or critical terms. You might develop an earlier point, introduce a contrasting perspective, or use the second source to complicate what the first one suggested.
04
Land on a position
~50 words
Conclude with a clear statement that is recognisably your own. Not a summary of what you've read, but a position you've arrived at through the thinking you've done in this entry.

This structure is a guide, not a template. If your thinking takes a different shape — especially in visual or video entries — that's fine. What matters is that we can see the progression from provocation to research to your own position.

Annotated examples

What strong entries look like

The examples below come from a previous version of this subject, where students chose their own topics more freely. In the current version, each entry must grow out of a specific provocation from the module videos. However, these examples are useful for showing the register we're looking for, how external sources can be woven into your thinking, and the way a position develops across an entry.

Read them for the quality of the thinking and writing, not as templates for topic selection.

A note on these examples: The colour coding identifies the four key moves in each entry — starting from the material, bringing in external sources, and arriving at a position. Each example demonstrates a slightly different approach to structuring these moves, which is exactly the kind of variation we welcome.
Submission details

Final notes

Your journal is submitted as a single document at the end of the semester. Entries 1–3 are standalone responses to different module groups — each one should work on its own terms. Entry 4 is where you step back and draw connections across what you've encountered in the subject, showing how your thinking has developed over the semester.

At key points during the semester, you'll submit drafts through FeedbackFruits and exchange feedback with your peers. This is built into the assessment: the Peer Engagement criterion recognises students who have genuinely participated in this exchange and used it to refine their work.

Total length
~1,200 words (4 × 300), or equivalent
Format
PDF or Word, 12pt, 1.5 or double spacing
Referencing
Chicago 17 Author–Date
Weighting
30% of final grade

Please adhere to basic conventions in spelling, formatting, and capitalisation. If you have hand-written or illustrated your journal, scan the pages clearly. For video entries, upload as MP4 or provide a streaming link alongside any written components.

If you have questions about the journal, raise them in tutorials or contact your tutor.
